claims.text: Controlled thermal oxidation of the catalyst will selectively segregate platinum-group metals to the surface.
The treatment will produce a continuous, nanometer-scale, noble-metal-rich surface layer.
The noble-metal-rich layer will improve low-temperature oxidation performance.
The noble-metal-rich layer will enhance resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
The noble-metal-rich layer will increase durability during simulated vehicle aging relative to the untreated catalyst.
A treatment at approximately 150–200 °C for 1–2 hours in 5–10% O2, followed by cooling in an oxygen-poor atmosphere, is sufficient to create the proposed surface structure.
The proposed effects will persist during cyclic H2O and NO exposure at temperatures up to 300 °C for 100–200 hours.
Moderate thermal treatment gives platinum-group-metal atoms sufficient mobility to segregate to the surface.
The segregated platinum-group metals form surface oxides or metallic clusters.
The segregated surface species are inherently active for low-temperature oxidation.
The segregated surface species resist deleterious adsorption of H2O and NO.
The noble-metal-rich surface protects the underlying alloy matrix from sintering or degradation.
The treated catalyst will have a light-off temperature below 150 °C.
The treated catalyst will undergo less H2O- and NO-induced deactivation than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will retain activity better than the untreated catalyst over the specified aging period.
Treatment outside 150–200 °C or the stated oxygen concentration risks over-oxidation, nonuniform layer formation, or active-site blockage.
Over-oxidation, nonuniform layer formation, or active-site blockage could negate the performance gains.

contradictions.description: The catalyst is described as near-equiatomic in constituents including Pd and/or Pt, but Pd/Pt are also called minor platinum-group metals. If they are principal near-equiatomic constituents, characterizing them as minor is inconsistent without a more precise composition.
The treatment atmosphere is described as both air and 5–10% O2; ordinary air contains about 21% O2, so the intended balance gas is unclear.
